wa_mount_rahm_south_side.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side
wa_mount_rahm_south_side.notes: The unmaintained Depot Creek trail crosses the border to Ouzel Lake, then the bench leads east to the south side. The easiest and most used way, but it means crossing the border on foot away from a port of entry, so confirm the entry rules first, and the road needs high clearance.
hazards: Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
No rappel anchors reported in the crux gully; it must be downclimbed
Steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy early season
Border crossing on foot away from a port of entry; high-clearance road to the trailhead
Ouzel Lake camp reached by an unmaintained trail; Custer-Spickard saddle and terrace traverse are cross-country

wa_mount_rahm_south_side.name: Silver Creek from Ross Lake
wa_mount_rahm_south_side.notes: The all-US way: a water taxi up Ross Lake to the mouth of Silver Creek, then a long bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake and north to the upper terrace. Harder and much brushier.
hazards: Long, brushy bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake; harder than the other way in
Water taxi up Ross Lake needed to reach the mouth of Silver Creek
Climbing above lakeside cliffs or talus and slabs to reach the upper terrace
Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
No rappel anchors reported in the crux gully; steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy early season
wa_mount_rahm_south_side.whyThisWay: When staying entirely within the United States, avoiding the foot crossing of the border and the rough road to Depot Creek, at the cost of a boat ride and a long bushwhack.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
hazards: Boat access from Ross Lake Resort must be booked; no road out if plans slip
Slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin at 2,900 ft
Loose moraine between the lake and the glacier toe
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Silver Glacier; the glacier is thinning so lines shift yearly
Class 4 summit-block step on loose, lichen-covered rock
Long, committing retreat from a high camp
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.whyThisWay: To keep the whole trip inside the United States with no border crossing on foot, for parties willing to book a water taxi up Ross Lake and push through the cross-country above the cabin.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.baseFinding:
From the Silver Lake camp the route does not go near a col. Walk round the north side of the lake to its far, south-west end, then head south across moraine and snow, skirting a small rock buttress, to the toe of the glacier at about 7,400 ft. Allow an hour to an hour and a half from camp.

You should be able to see at least the lower glacier from camp, so pick your line onto it before you leave. The ice comes down toward the lake from the north side of the peak; you rope up at its toe and climb it, with no saddle or gully on the way.

The wide gully and the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west belong to the other approach, from the lake on the Depot Creek side. If you are climbing a gully toward a gap, you have left this line.

And the negative marker that matters most: the south-west route on this peak starts at the toe of a different glacier on the other flank, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
hazards: International border crossing on foot; passports needed
Wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at Depot Creek Falls, the crux of the walk-in
Overgrown approach road that washes out and lengthens the walk
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Silver Glacier beyond the Custer-Spickard saddle
Class 4 summit-block step on loose, lichen-covered rock
Taking the wrong route from the shared Ouzel Lake camp costs a day
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.baseFinding:
From the Depot Creek camp, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the col.

The fixed point is the same: the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully you came up is the way back to camp; the glacier lies on the far side.

The test that you are at the right gap is that both summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

Do not confuse this start with the south-west route, which leaves the same camp. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. If you have not gained a col, you are not on this route.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
hazards: Border crossing on foot; passport needed, with a register at the obelisk
Washed-out road lengthens the walk without warning
Wet slick boulders and slabs at Depot Creek Falls with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
Crevasses on the southwest glacier, including a marginal snow bridge on the standard line
Short steep loose rock gully at the glacier head, then loose Class 2-3 ribs and gullies near the summit
30-40 degree snow near the summit ridge
Extreme remoteness, no cell coverage
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.baseFinding:
The critical instruction is that you leave the drainage before the pass, not at it. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but well before reaching that saddle, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

The negative marker is exact and easy to use: if you have arrived at the saddle and are looking down into the cirque on the far side, you have gone too far. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

The buttress toe is the feature - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

The base is the toe of the south-west glacier, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across. The line up the ice is its climber's-right margin, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

Confirm at the top of the ice: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
hazards: Boat access must be booked; no road out
Slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin at 2,900 ft
Long carry to a high camp at about 6,763 ft
Crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide, including a marginal snow bridge on the southwest glacier
Short steep loose rock gully at the glacier head and loose Class 2-3 rock near the summit
Camp is on the opposite side from Depot Creek, so col-based descriptions can mislead
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.whyThisWay: To keep the whole trip inside the United States with no border crossing on foot, for parties who will book a water taxi up Ross Lake and handle the long cross-country approach.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.baseFinding:
The old cabin at about 2,900 ft is the proof you are on the right side of the creek. The trail climbs the north side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

Above the cabin the markers are occasional blazes on trees rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

The camp is the lake basin at about 6,763 ft, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

Be clear which route you are on when you arrive. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. The south-west route instead wants the toe of the south-west glacier, which is reached by traversing into open heather and moraine basins round the toe of a rock buttress, not by gaining a col. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.

wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.baseFinding:
The col between the two Mox summits is the whole navigation, and the trap is that there are two summits. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

At the col, check which tower you are under. This route is on the eastern summit, which is the harder and higher of the pair. If the peak above you is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, you are facing the western summit and have turned the wrong way out of the saddle.

The sequence above the col is a ladder of specific shapes, in order, and it is how you know you are right: a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief descent to a small flat area. The flat spot after a downclimb is the confirmation - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

From that flat area, locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. If you are uncoiling a rope at the col itself, you are hundreds of feet too low.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.whyThisWay: When the glacier is in good shape and the weather is settled, a party moves up to the saddle camp for a much shorter summit day instead of staying at the lake.
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.baseFinding:
From either camp the route meets at the same place: the saddle between the two Mox summits, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

The high camp's own marker is that it sits on rock outcrops at the glacier's edge at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

At the saddle, the summit you want is the eastern one - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

The confirmation sequence is the same ladder: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short downclimb to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing depends on a cable car being in service; serious ford if not
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt can be committing
Steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread above Bear Creek
Loose south-facing slopes on the divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the shrinking glacier in the couloir
Moat between neve and slab worsens through the season
Days from any road; loose, hard-to-protect rock on the buttress
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.baseFinding:
The route begins by losing height, and that is the single most important thing to know at camp. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. Any line that climbs upward from the saddle toward rock is the wrong one.

Identify the saddle first: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

At the ice, the positive test is which side of the buttress you go up. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the climber's-left side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. The toe of the buttress itself, where the rock meets the ice on the right-hand side, is the start of the direct and not of this route. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

Watch the join between snow and rock. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A cross-check once committed: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively the only high camp for the buttress, in heather meadow a little below the notch on the northwest ridge, where scattered trees give some wind shelter and flat grassy ground. Reached by climbing roughly 3,000 ft out of the Bear Creek valley to treeline on a rough climbers' path through open forest that gives way to blueberry brush. Around nine hours from the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side; the American approach over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River is far longer, on the order of seventeen miles, but is the one that keeps the permit straightforward. Expect mosquitoes.
bivy.water: Running water at the camp, fed by semi-permanent snowfields just above; those patches are described as holding meltwater well into the later part of the season.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, Bear Mountain cross-country zone: maximum party of six and six permits per night. This zone cannot be reserved in advance — it is walk-up only, from the Wilderness Information Center. Cross-country camping is restricted to durable ground.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count. The binding number is the permit: six people per party, six parties a night in the zone.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: Border crossing on foot with no port of entry; legality unconfirmed
Unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
Loose south-facing slopes on the divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant beneath the buttress
Loose, hard-to-protect rock on the buttress
Remote position; a rescue may involve two countries
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.whyThisWay: Only for parties already in Canada who have confirmed a lawful border crossing; much shorter, but the tread is overgrown after the first mile or two.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.baseFinding:
The approach variant changes only how you arrive at the 6,480 ft saddle. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by dropping off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

The same two tests apply at the ice. Go up the snow on the climber's-left side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

And the same negative marker: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

wa_direct_north_buttress.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_direct_north_buttress.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
wa_direct_north_buttress.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing in high water; cable car or ford
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
Steep brushy timber, slide alder and a loose divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir below the wall
Deep moat at the toe of the buttress late season
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Remote and committing, several days from help
wa_direct_north_buttress.baseFinding:
The Direct starts at the very bottom of the rock, and that is what separates it from the route it shares a camp with. From the saddle you first go down: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

The toe of the buttress lies on the right-hand side of that ice, where the rock runs down into the snow. That junction is the start. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

The negative marker is unambiguous and it is the common mistake: the regular North Buttress walks past this toe and continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. If you are still walking on snow with the buttress rising to your right, you have walked past the Direct and are heading for the regular start. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A second check is how soon it gets hard. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

Watch the moat at the junction. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

wa_direct_north_buttress.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. The alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is shorter, but the cross-border stretch can be heavy bushwhacking, so the long trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

wa_direct_north_buttress.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
wa_direct_north_buttress.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: International border crossing on foot
Overgrown, unmaintained tread; heavy bushwhacking on the cross-border stretch
Same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall below the buttress
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Cross-border rescue complications; remote and committing
wa_direct_north_buttress.whyThisWay: For parties already in Canada, as it is a much shorter walk to the saddle camp, but it crosses the border on foot away from a port of entry and is not a lawful way in for everyone.
wa_direct_north_buttress.baseFinding:
Arrival differs, the start does not. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

Tie in at the toe of the rock on the right-hand side of the ice, where the buttress runs down into the snow and there is no more snow above you. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.

hazards: Boat crossing of Ross Lake needed; a long multi-day approach with a retreat measured in days

wa_north_face_left_buttress.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Wildfires close this road and parts of the northern wilderness in some summers, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
bivy.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
bivy.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
bivy.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
bivy.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
bivy.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.

Harts Pass road is single lane, steep and exposed; usually opens only in July; wildfire can close it
Snow lingering on north-facing traverses into August; sparse water along the crest

Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face; descent by the east ridge and snow finger
wa_north_face_left_buttress.whyThisWay: When no boat is available and you want to stay in the United States; it is about 27 miles each way along the crest from Harts Pass, which usually opens only in July.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Multi-day approach by boat and abandoned, brushy trail; steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the junction
Several unmarked routes on a 1,400 ft wall; identification is by position under the summit only
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall, worst once sun hits the face
Dirt- and moss-filled cracks mid-route and teetering blocks near the top
No cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
hazards: The described line crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides, one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face; loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Retreat from anywhere on the trip is measured in days
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

From that view, drop a plumb line from the summit. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the rockfall line rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

Negative marker: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
