wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a road that has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025 (before that it was often snowed shut into early or mid July), and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.
hazards: Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's ice cliffs onto the traverse between camp and the bergschrund
Bergschrund and crevasses at the start of the technical ground, around 9,800 ft
Bare rock at the 5.6 crux chimney in lean years raises both the grade and the rockfall
Rockfall off decomposing volcanic cliffs on everything below about 12,200 ft
Overhanging rock step on the knife-edge crest into high camp; sustained 45 to 60 degree snow and ice with a long exposed traverse
No road access to Mowich Lake since the April 2025 bridge closure, and a descent that finishes at a different trailhead
Remote, rarely-traveled route: slow rescue
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.baseFinding: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet below it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately east of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops west off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back east, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: The high camp the route is climbed from, on the crest of Ptarmigan Ridge near 10,000 ft. Exposed to wind; no running water.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites on the ridge crest

bivy.name: White River Campground
bivy.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
bivy.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.
hazards: Hours of exposure to rockfall and icefall crossing beneath Willis Wall and the Liberty Wall
Crevasses on the Winthrop and the Carbon: thin bridges early, open cracks late
Committing traverse with no quick exit once past Curtis Ridge
Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's cliffs onto the traverse into the route
Sustained 45 to 60 degree ice and a rock or mixed crux around 12,000 ft
Very little traffic, so no established track above the Carbon and a slow rescue
Losing the faint Emmons descent to the well-trodden Disappointment Cleaver at the summit
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.whyThisWay: When the Mowich Lake road is closed or snowed in, and for parties without a car shuttle, since it returns to the White River car after the Emmons descent; longer and crosses more glaciers.
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.baseFinding: This is the approach on which Rainier's two Liberty Cap routes actually get confused, and the trap is a physical one: there is usually a bootpack running from St. Elmo Pass to the Carbon Glacier, and it was stamped in by parties going to Liberty Ridge. It is the right track as far as the Carbon and the wrong one after that. Working west you cross under Willis Wall and meet a narrow rock and snow ridge dropping straight to the glacier. That first spine is Liberty Ridge. Keep going. Past it the ground opens beneath a big pale cirque wall capped by hanging ice, and the next crest beyond that wall, roughly a mile and a half further west, is Ptarmigan Ridge. Put it the simple way and it is hard to get wrong: on Liberty Ridge the Liberty Wall is on your right, and on Ptarmigan Ridge it is on your left. Cross the Carbon below the seracs, gain the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge up to the flat high camp at 10,200 to 10,300 ft. That flat is the base of the climb, and four things fix it together: room for a couple of small tents, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon immediately east, banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and Liberty Ridge in full view straight across. From camp the route drops west off the crest onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, near a rock outcropping about the middle of the face — study that crossing from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there. Above the schrund the line rises back east, climber's left, toward the ice cliffs. If you have crossed a schrund with no ice cliff up and left of you, you are on the wrong part of the mountain.

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently on April 22, 2025, so this start cannot be reached by car
hazards: Mowich Lake road has no public access since April 2025; this start is unavailable
Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp; site camp outside the serac fall line
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier; verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Crevasse fall crossing the Mowich or Winthrop glaciers; avalanche-prone approach slopes on the Mowich/Carbon side
Committing, remote position with a carry-over descent by the Emmons-Winthrop
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.whyThisWay: In early summer once its road is open, for a shorter walk in, if a car shuttle to the White River end can be arranged, since the usual descent comes out there.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you descend, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers; crossing the Carbon
Long committing traverse with no quick exit; much longer approach
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Bergschrund and upper mixed ground; verglassed rock and water ice late season
Carry-over descent by the Emmons-Winthrop through large crevasses
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)

bivy.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
bivy.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.

bivy.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
bivy.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the account.
bivy.water: A tarn at the saddle, and it is the weak point — it is stagnant, and parties have found frog and mosquito larvae in it. Better water is a short way above, around 5,500 ft, where small streams cascade down; fill there rather than at the pond.
bivy.capacity: Four to six tents, so leave room for another party.

bivy.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
bivy.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. The Corkscrew from Bedal Creek is a reasonable single day of thirteen or fourteen hours for a fit party, and successful ascents in under twelve hours are common, so the usual pattern is to sleep at the trailhead and start around four in the morning rather than carry a camp to the ridge.
bivy.water: Carry it, or take it from Bedal Creek on the way in.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass is usually reported as the required parking permit, though not universally; carry one.
bivy.capacity: Roadside parking, not a designated site.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
hazards: Rough, narrow FR 4096 spur; high clearance helps
Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in a brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block, worse with parties stacked in the gully
Low-5th-class exposed step about 100 ft below the summit, downclimbed on the way back
Moat falls on the glacier edge have caused a documented accident
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your right for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk: deep, cold and fast in early season; log jams move year to year
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block, worse with parties stacked in the gully
Low-5th-class exposed step about 100 ft below the summit, downclimbed on the way back
Moat falls on the glacier edge have caused a documented accident
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.whyThisWay: Later in July and August when the river is low, or if the rough spur road to the Bedal trailhead is impassable or the climbers' path turn off the old trail worries the party.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your right, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.hours: 2.5-3.5 for the Lake Constance trail alone
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations for the May 15-October 15 summer season; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
hazards: fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses
steep firm snow on the Terrible Traverse - several pickets advised in early season
exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands on the Lake Constance trail above 1.3 miles
loose talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
no water above the lake in late summer, and Constance Creek itself runs dry
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.baseFinding:
From the lake, follow the boot path around the shore, out onto a large scree cone, and north into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance. A large rock called the Thumb sits on the canyon's left side; the South Chute lies on the south side of the Thumb, and due south of the Cat Ears.

The most useful rule on this mountain: start up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears come into view, not when the chute starts to look obvious. Entering low keeps you on firmer ground, where there is a path in places; parties who keep walking up the canyon and attack the chute higher get the worst of the loose scree. If the Cat Ears have been visible for a while and you are still walking north, you have overshot the entrance.

From the lake the chute line climbs roughly 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. Descend about 150 ft, then a second gully leads to a notch near 7,300 ft.

Above that is the exposed upper maze, and identifying which traverse you are on is the thing to get right. The Finger Traverse is a downsloping ledge above a cliff with old rusted pitons on it — the pitons are the identifier, and some parties clip them as a solo-belay anchor. The Terrible Traverse is a hard-snow traverse of roughly 45 degrees above a big cliff and a nasty drainage. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, ground leading to the base of the summit block. If you are on a traverse and the summit block is not visible above and ahead of you, you are on the wrong ledge.

The actual climbing is only the summit block, about 60 ft, with the North Chimney taking its north side at 3rd class — reported by plenty of people as feeling like easy 4th.

wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.notes:
The roughly 5 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the signed start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.
hazards: old roadbed surface with washouts
everything above the bike drop is unchanged, including the exposed ledges on the Lake Constance path
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.whyThisWay: To cut the long road walk at both ends of the trip, leaving the bike at the start of the climbers' path; the climb above is the same.
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.baseFinding: Unchanged from the walk-in: around the lake, north into Avalanche Canyon, and up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears appear above you, with the Thumb on the canyon's left marking the chute's south side. The Cat Ears becoming visible is the trigger to start climbing, not a landmark to walk toward.
